complexity: Usually O(n) time and O(n) extra space - the space is what buys the speed.

ideas.text: Walk once; before storing x, ask whether its partner is already stored.
ideas.title: Seen-set / complement map

ideas.text: Map each item to a key shared by everything in its group (sorted letters, counts).
ideas.title: Canonical key

ideas.text: A dict or a 26-slot array of counts answers 'same letters?' and 'most frequent?'.
ideas.title: Counting

ideas.text: Precompute running totals so each answer is O(1).
ideas.title: Prefix products/sums

name: Arrays & Hashing
signals: "Have I seen this before?" - duplicates, complements, pairs
Grouping things that are equivalent under some transformation
Counting occurrences or frequencies
An O(n) answer is expected and sorting isn't required
summary: Most brute-force array solutions re-scan data they've already looked at. A hash map or set remembers it instead, turning an O(n) search into an O(1) lookup - and an O(n²) algorithm into O(n).
tagline: Trade memory for time: remember what you've seen.
template:
seen = {}                      # value -> index (or count, or group)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    if want(x) in seen:        # ask before you store
        return seen[want(x)], i
    seen[x] = i

complexity: O(n) per scan, O(1) extra space. Add O(n log n) if you sort first.

ideas.text: Start at both ends; the comparison tells you which end can't be part of a better answer.
ideas.title: Converging pointers

ideas.text: When a value is capped by the smaller of two sides, the smaller side is the one to move.
ideas.title: Move the bottleneck

ideas.text: For k-sum, fix one element and run two pointers on the rest.
ideas.title: Anchor + squeeze

ideas.text: After sorting, equal values are adjacent - skip them to avoid duplicate answers.
ideas.title: Skip duplicates

name: Two Pointers
signals: Sorted input, or input you can sort
Pairs/triplets with a target sum
Palindromes and other mirror checks
Something is bounded by the shorter/smaller of two ends
summary: Instead of checking every pair (i, j), keep two indices and move one of them based on a comparison. Each move rules out every pair involving the discarded position, so n moves cover all n² pairs.
tagline: Two indices moving with purpose eliminate whole rows of pairs at once.

complexity: O(n): each element enters and leaves the window once. Space is the window summary.

ideas.text: for r: add s[r]; while invalid: remove s[l], l += 1; update the answer.
ideas.title: Variable window

ideas.text: When the size is fixed, each slide adds one element and removes one: O(1) updates.
ideas.title: Fixed window

ideas.text: Find a cheap test for 'window is valid' - e.g. len − maxFreq ≤ k.
ideas.title: Validity formula

ideas.text: Keep candidates in decreasing order to read the window max in O(1).
ideas.title: Monotonic deque

name: Sliding Window
signals: "Longest/shortest contiguous substring or subarray such that …"
A condition you can repair by removing elements from the left
Fixed-size windows: "every window of length k"
Counts of characters inside a range
summary: For contiguous subarrays or substrings, keep a window [l, r] with a running summary (a set, counts, a sum). Extend r to explore; when the window breaks a rule, advance l until it's valid again. Both pointers only move forward, so the 'nested' loop is O(n) in total.
tagline: Grow to explore, shrink to repair - and never move backwards.
template:
window = Counter()
l = best = 0
for r, x in enumerate(s):
    window[x] += 1
    while invalid(window):
        window[s[l]] -= 1
        l += 1
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)

complexity: Monotonic stacks are O(n) total: every index is pushed once and popped at most once.

ideas.text: A closer must match the most recent unmatched opener - the top of the stack.
ideas.title: Match the top

ideas.text: Keep the stack sorted; a new element pops everything it resolves. Each item is pushed and popped once.
ideas.title: Monotonic stack

ideas.text: Store extra info (like the running minimum) with every element.
ideas.title: Augmented stack

ideas.text: Numbers wait on the stack; operators consume the top two.
ideas.title: Operand stack

name: Stack
signals: Matching pairs and nesting
"Next greater/smaller element", spans, waiting times
Evaluating expressions
Undo / backtracking, or a min/max that must survive pops
summary: Stacks model nesting and 'most recent unmatched' relationships: brackets, expression evaluation, and the monotonic stack, where each element waits until something larger (or smaller) arrives to resolve it.
tagline: The most recent unfinished thing is the one that matters next.

complexity: O(log n) probes. Searching an answer space of size M with an O(n) check costs O(n log M).

ideas.text: Decide what lo and hi mean (answer is in [lo, hi]) and make every update preserve it.
ideas.title: Keep the invariant

ideas.text: When the input isn't sorted but the answer space is, binary-search the answer with a feasibility test.
ideas.title: Search the answer

ideas.text: In a rotated array one half of every split is sorted - check it first.
ideas.title: Find the sorted half

ideas.text: For 'first x that works', keep hi on a known-good x and stop when lo == hi.
ideas.title: Leftmost true

name: Binary Search
signals: Sorted (or rotated-sorted) input and an O(log n) target
"Find the smallest x such that …" or "the largest x that still …"
A feasibility check that gets easier as a number grows (speed, capacity, days)
Lookups by timestamp or position in data that only ever grows in order
summary: Binary search isn't really about sorted arrays - it's about any yes/no question whose answers flip exactly once along a range. Probe the middle, learn which side of the flip you're on, discard the other half. log₂ of a billion is 30, so 30 probes find anything.
tagline: Every comparison throws away half of what's left.

complexity: Typically O(n) time and O(1) extra space - the nodes already exist; you only move arrows.

ideas.text: A node before the head removes every 'what if it's the first node?' special case.
ideas.title: Dummy node

ideas.text: nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev, curr = curr, nxt.
ideas.title: Save, flip, step

ideas.text: Speeds 1 and 2 find the middle, detect cycles, and locate a cycle's entrance.
ideas.title: Fast & slow

ideas.text: Start one pointer n nodes ahead to find the n-th node from the end in one pass.
ideas.title: Gap pointers

name: Linked List
signals: Reverse, reorder, or remove nodes in place
Cycle detection or finding the middle
Merging sorted lists
O(1) extra space on a sequence
summary: Linked list problems are about rewiring next pointers without losing anything. A handful of moves cover almost everything: a dummy head, save-flip-advance reversal, fast/slow pointers, and merging.
tagline: It's all pointer surgery - draw the arrows before you move them.
template:
dummy = ListNode(0, head)
prev, curr = None, head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next         # 1. save
    curr.next = prev        # 2. flip
    prev, curr = curr, nxt  # 3. step
return prev
